newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Fall in Philippine peso to drive up grain imports.
newsitem.headline: Fall in Philippine peso to drive up grain imports.

text.p: The devaluation of the Philippine peso will drive up the cost of wheat and corn imports, but Manila is seen taking the increases in stride because of robust demand for those products, grains analysts and traders said on Friday.
"The devaluation would certainly prompt big flour mills to re-evaluate their imports," a senior grains industry analyst in Singapore said.
The peso dived 11.5 percent to 29.45 to the dollar after the Philippine Central Bank announced on Friday it would allow the local unit to move in a wider range.

U.S. Wheat Associates, the marketing arm for the U.S. wheat industry, said the Philippines imported about 2.1 million tonnes of the grain in the 1996/97 marketing year, 1.8 million of which came from the United States.
Manila is expected to import 2.1 million tonnes in 1997/98 as demand for wheat products is likely remain strong.

The country buys mostly hard red spring and soft white wheat. It uses the wheat for a basic round bread called the 'pan de sal' consumed at breakfast and to meet rapidly growing demand from the fast food industry in the country.

"I think they'll import the same amount of wheat. The question really is whether the flour mills there can work on lower margins. I think the demand is there that would support some price increases," one trader said.
Another dealer felt the volume of Philippine wheat imports "will not really fall that drastically. At most, it would be five percent."
"I think wheat products in the Philippines are so basic they can afford a price bump," he added.
One analyst, however, said the higher cost of imports may contribute to inflationary pressures in the country.
"This will definitely drive up their costs," he said.
Corn imports will also cost more and this would impact directly on poultry and livestock companies already bridling at the high price of domestic corn.
The Philippines is expected to import about 500,000 tonnes of corn this year, with most coming from the United States, China and Argentina.
"The corn imports are going to rise because of the increased demand of the processed food industry," one trader said.
